en: The Theravāda Vinaya:
Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga,
Pārājika Section
5. The Training Rule on Kneeling with Raised Knees Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, Sāḷha Migāra’s nephew desired to build a dwelling for the community of bhikkhunīs.
Then Sāḷha Migāra’s nephew approached the bhikkhunīs and said this:
“Noble ladies, I wish to build a dwelling for the community of bhikkhunīs.”
“Give me a nun who is a builder.
Now at that time, four sisters had gone forth among the bhikkhunīs:
Nandā, Nandavatī, Sundarīnandā, and Thullanandā.
Among them, the bhikkhunī Sundarīnandā was one who had gone forth while young; she was beautiful, pleasing to behold, and inspiring;
she was wise, competent, intelligent, skillful, and diligent, endowed with the investigative discernment necessary for such tasks, capable of acting and capable of organizing.
Then the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs, having formally authorized the bhikkhunī Sundarīnandā, appointed her as the overseer of construction work for Sāḷha, the grandson of Migāra.
Now at that time, the bhikkhunī Sundarīnandā used to go frequently to the residence of Sāḷha, the grandson of Migāra, saying, “Give me an adze;
give me an axe; give me a hatchet; give me a spade; give me a chisel.
Sāḷha, the grandson of Migāra, also used to go frequently to the bhikkhunīs’ quarters to see what had been done and what remained to be done.
Their minds became bound by the sight of her constantly.
Then Sāḷha, the grandson of Migāra, being unable to find an opportunity to violate the bhikkhunī Sundarīnandā, prepared a meal for the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs for that very purpose.
Then, while Sāḷha, the grandson of Migāra, was arranging the seats in the dining hall, he said: "There are so many bhikkhunīs [for this] lady..."
“For those who are older than Sundarīnandā,” he arranged seats to one side; “for those who are younger,” he arranged seats to one side.

He arranged a seat for the bhikkhunī Sundarīnandā in a concealed place, in a corner, so that the elder bhikkhunīs would know she was sitting near the junior bhikkhunīs; and the junior bhikkhunīs [also knew].
“They would know: ‘She is sitting in the presence of the elder bhikkhunīs.
Then Sāḷha, Migāra’s grandson, announced the time to the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs: ‘It is time, noble ladies; the meal is ready.
Sundarīnandā the bhikkhunī observed: ‘Sāḷha, Migāra’s grandson, has not prepared this meal for the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs out of respect; he wishes to defile me.’”
“If I go, I will be missed,” she thought, and she commanded her resident nun: “Go and bring me almsfood.
And if anyone asks for me, inform them that I am ill.
“Very well, Noble Lady,” that nun replied to the bhikkhunī Sundarīnandā.
Now at that time, Sāḷha Migāra’s nephew was standing outside the gateway questioning the bhikkhunī Sundarīnandā:
“Where, noble lady, is the noble lady Sundarīnandā? Where, noble lady, is the noble lady Sundarīnandā?
When this was said, the bhikkhunī who was the pupil of the bhikkhunī Sundarīnandā said to Sāḷha Migāra’s nephew: “She is ill, friend; I will bring her almsfood.”
Then Sāḷha, the grandson of Migāra, thinking, "I have had a meal prepared for the community of bhikkhunīs for the sake of the lady Sundarīnandā," gave orders to his men,
saying, "Serve the community of bhikkhunīs with food," and went to the bhikkhunīs' quarters.
At that time, the bhikkhunī Sundarīnandā was standing at the gate outside the monastery, waiting for Sāḷha, the grandson of Migāra.
The bhikkhunī Sundarīnandā saw Sāḷha, the grandson of Migāra, coming from afar. Upon seeing him, she entered her dwelling, covered her head with her robe, and lay down on the couch.
Then Sāḷha, the grandson of Migāra, approached the bhikkhunī Sundarīnandā; having approached, he said this to the bhikkhunī Sundarīnandā: “What is wrong with you, noble lady? Why are you lying down?
“It is indeed so, friend, for one who desires what another does not desire.”
“Noble lady, how could I not desire you?
However, I find no opportunity to defile you.
Thus, being lustful himself, he engaged in physical contact with the lustful bhikkhunī Sundarīnandā.
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhunī, frail with old age and suffering from a foot ailment, was lying not far from the bhikkhunī Sundarīnandā.
That bhikkhunī saw Sāḷha, the grandson of Migāra, who was lustful, engaging in physical contact with the lustful bhikkhunī Sundarīnandā.
Having seen this, she criticized, complained, and spread it about: “How can the noble lady Sundarīnandā, being lustful herself, consent to physical contact with a lustful man?”
Then that bhikkhunī reported this matter to the bhikkhunīs.
Those bhikkhunīs who were of few desires, contented, modest, scrupulous, and desirous of training, were indignant, disparaged [her], and complained:
"How can the noble lady Sundarīnandā, being lustful, consent to physical contact with a lustful man?"

Then those bhikkhunīs informed the bhikkhus of this matter. Those bhikkhus who were few in desires, contented, modest, scrupulous, and desirous of training, complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
"How can the bhikkhunī Sundarīnandā, being lustful, consent to physical contact with a lustful man?"
Then those bhikkhus, having rebuked the bhikkhunī Sundarīnandā in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, on that occasion and in that connection, having convened the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, questioned the bhikkhus:
“Is it true, bhikkhus, that the bhikkhunī Sundarīnandā, being lustful, consented to physical contact with a lustful man?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked her:
“It is unbecoming, monks, for the bhikkhunī Sundarīnandā; it is unsuitable, improper, unworthy of a recluse, unallowable, and not to be done.”
"How indeed, monks, could the nun Sundarīnandā, being lustful, consent to physical contact with a lustful man?
This, monks, is neither for the inspiration of those without faith nor for the increase of those who have faith.
On the contrary, monks, it leads to the lack of faith in those without faith, and to the alienation of some among those who have faith."
Then the Blessed One, having rebuked the bhikkhunī Sundarīnandā in many ways,
and having spoken in dispraise of being difficult to support, difficult to maintain, of great desires, lack of contentment, socializing, and laziness;
and having in many ways spoken in praise of being easy to support, easy to maintain, of fewness of wishes, contentment, effacement, and the ascetic practices—
Having spoken in praise of inspiring conduct, the decline of evil, and the arousal of energy,
and having given the monks a Dhamma talk appropriate and conducive thereto,
he addressed the monks: "Therefore, monks, I shall lay down a training rule for the nuns based on ten reasons."
For the well-being of the Saṅgha, for the comfort of the Saṅgha, for the restraint of wayward bhikkhunīs, for the ease of well-behaved bhikkhunīs,
for the restraint of taints pertaining to the present life, for the warding off of taints pertaining to future lives,
for the inspiration of those without faith, for the increase of those with faith, for the endurance of the true Dhamma, and for the support of the Vinaya.
And furthermore, monks, the nuns should recite this training rule:
“Whichever nun, being lustful, should consent to being touched, stroked, grasped, contacted, or pressed by a lustful man below the collarbone and above the knees, she too— ”
"She is one who has committed a *pārājika* offense, is no longer in communion, and is one whose thighs have been exposed. As for the phrase "but she who":

whoever she may be—of whatever kind, as described, of whatever birth, whatever name, whatever clan, whatever character, whatever mode of dwelling, whatever range of activity, whether senior, junior, or of middle standing—this is what is meant by "but she who."
"Bhikkhunī" means one who seeks alms is a bhikkhunī;
one who has entered upon the practice of alms-gathering is a bhikkhunī.
A "bhikkhunī" is so called because she wears torn robes;
a "bhikkhunī" by common designation;
a "bhikkhunī" by formal admission.
A bhikkhunī is so called because she says, "Come, bhikkhunī";
a bhikkhunī is one who is fully ordained through the threefold going for refuge;
a bhikkhunī is a noble woman.
A bhikkhunī who is a core;
a bhikkhunī who is in training;
a bhikkhunī who is beyond training.

A bhikkhunī is one who has received full ordination through a formal act consisting of a motion and a third proclamation (*ñatticatuttha-kamma*), performed by a complete assembly of both Sanghas—an act that is irreversible and fit for its purpose.
In this context, the term "bhikkhunī" refers specifically to one who has received full ordination through such a formal act performed by a complete assembly of both Sanghas.
"A lustful woman" (*avassutā*) means...
"Passionate" means having regard [for the object] and having a mind bound [to it].
One who is "corrupted" is one who is passionate, has regard, and has a mind bound [to it].
A "person" (purisapuggala) means a human male, not a *yakkha*, not a *peta*, and not an animal; one who is conscious and capable of engaging in physical contact.
"Below the collarbone" (*adhakkhaka*)...
"Below the collarbone.
"Above the kneecaps" means the area above the kneecaps.
"Touching" means merely touching. "Grasping" means...
And from here and there is the drawing together.
Grasping means merely that which has been grasped.
"Kissing" means merely touching.
"Or should consent to being pressed" means...
Having grasped a limb, one consents to being squeezed.
"This too" is said with reference to the preceding [cases].
"She becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense" means:
just as, for example, a man whose head is cut off is incapable of living by means of that bodily frame,
even so a lustful nun who touches a lustful male person below the collarbone and above the knees [commits a *pārājika*].
If she consents to being touched, grasped, seized, stroked, or pressed, she is no longer a *samaṇī*, no longer a daughter of the Sakyans.
Therefore, it is said that she has committed a *pārājika* offense. She is one who is not in communion (*asaṃvāsā*).
"Living together" means performing formal acts together, reciting the scriptures together, and training under the same rules—this is what is meant by "living together.
Since he does not have that with her, it is called "not living together.
If, when both are lustful, he touches her body with his own body below the collarbone but above the knees, there is an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika).
If one touches what is connected to the body with the body, there is an offense of thullaccaya.
If one touches the body with what is connected to the body, there is an offense of thullaccaya.
If one touches what is connected to the body with what is connected to the body, there is an offense of dukkaṭa.
If she touches her own body with something that entails forfeiture, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she touches what is attached to her body with something that entails forfeiture, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she touches something that entails forfeiture with something that entails forfeiture, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she touches her body with her body above the collarbone and below the knees, it is an offense of thullaccaya.
If she touches what is connected to the body with her body, it is an offense of dukkaṭa.
If she touches her body with what is connected to the body, it is an offense of dukkaṭa.
If one touches what is attached to the body with what is attached to the body, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one touches the body with something that has been relinquished (nissaggiya), there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one touches what is attached to the body with something that has been relinquished, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one touches what is to be forfeited with what is to be forfeited, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If, while both are free from desire, one touches body with body below the collarbone and above the knees, there is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*).
If one touches what is connected to the body with the body, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she touches her body with something connected to her own body, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If she touches something connected to another’s body with something connected to her own body, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she touches her body with something that has been relinquished (nissaggiya), there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one touches something attached to the body with something that is subject to forfeiture, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one touches something subject to forfeiture with something subject to forfeiture, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one touches body against body above the collarbone or below the knees, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one touches what is connected to the body with the body, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one touches the body with what is connected to the body, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one touches what is connected to the body with what is connected to the body, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she touches her own body with something that entails forfeiture, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If she touches something attached to her body with something that entails forfeiture, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she touches something that entails forfeiture with something that entails forfeiture, there is an offense of wrong-doing.

If one who is lustful on both sides touches with his own body the body—below the collarbone and above the knees—of a male spirit (*yakkha*), a hungry ghost (*peta*), a paṇḍaka, or a human being in animal form, it is a *thullaccaya* offense.
If he touches what is connected to the body with his own body, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If he touches his own body with something connected to the body, it is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she touches what is attached to the body with what is attached to her own body, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If she touches the body with what has been relinquished (nissaggiya), there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she touches what is attached to the body with what has been relinquished, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one touches an article that ought to be forfeited with an article that ought to be forfeited, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one touches the body with the body above the collarbone and below the knees, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one touches something connected to the body with the body, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she touches her body with something connected to her own body, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If she touches something connected to another’s body with something connected to her own body, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she touches her body with something that has been relinquished (nissaggiya), there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she touches something attached to the body with something that is subject to forfeiture, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If she touches something subject to forfeiture with something subject to forfeiture, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If, while both are not lustful, she touches body with body below the collar bone and above the knees, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she touches what is connected to the body with her own body, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If she touches the body with what is connected to the body, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she touches what is connected to the body with what is connected to the body, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one touches the body with what is subject to forfeiture, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one touches what is attached to the body with what is subject to forfeiture, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one touches what is subject to forfeiture with what is subject to forfeiture, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one touches the body with the body above the collarbone and below the knees, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one touches what is connected to the body with the body, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one touches the body with what is connected to the body, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one touches what is connected to the body with what is connected to the body, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one touches the body with what has been relinquished (nissaggiya), there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one touches what is connected to the body with what has been relinquished, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one touches an article that ought to be forfeited with another article that ought to be forfeited, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense if it was unintentional.
through lack of mindfulness,
through not knowing,
through not consenting,
For one who is insane,
for one whose mind is deranged,
for one overwhelmed by pain,
"Regarding the first offender":
thus ends the First Pārājika.
